Wednesday, September 15, 2021

Testimony in support of Commercial Rent Stabilization

My first job after college, I worked as a seamstress for an amazing wedding dress designer
who’d had her shop on the LES for decades and had so much wisdom and amazing stories to
share. I felt so lucky to be able to learn from her but also to have such a deep connection to the
NYC that I loved so much as a child and wanted to live in as an adult. After decades in the
same space, working nonstop and living hand to mouth but loving it, her landlord decided to
raise her rent from $2,500 to $25,000 a month, leaving her without a business. (That is not a
typo.) As a working class artist without a 401k, she had no way to retire - but more importantly at
65 she still felt inspired to work and didn't want to retire. But no one can make a living paying
$25,000 a month, and so she had to close her business leaving her with few avenues to sustain
her life in NYC after that.

Sadly this story isn't unique. I’ve known too many community spaces and neighbors and friends
who’ve lost their businesses, livelihoods, life’s work; communities that lost our spaces and
neighborhood souls; because NYC has no regulation to protect commercial renters like we have
for residential renters.

Commercial rent stabilization has been something people have been talking about for years but
seemed impossible, but COVID laid bare how fragile everything is and there’s finally
momentum. the public supports this. Not just commercial renters either. If we don't protect what
makes NYC great, we'll lose the ability to attract visitors, which effects the entire economy.
Business owners who own their buildings support this because if their neighborhoods are full of
vacant storefronts it ruins their business and their community as well. Customers and neighbors
and regular folk need our communities intact.

One last story, why it’s important to have spaces in our neighborhoods that are rooted in the
community where we can form bonds over time. When my mom was 4, my grandma Minnie
wanted to give her her first haircut. My mom didn’t want to get her hair cut so she ran away and
hid in the local corner store, down the block from their house in Whitestone, Queens. The
shopkeeper knew her, and knew my grandma, and called Minnie to let her know her daughter
was safe. This can’t happen when our neighborhood spaces are constantly being replaced by
new businesses who are willing to pay more; and this can’t happen with empty storefronts.

Please use this moment to do what NYC should have done decades ago and protect our
commercial renters so NYC can continue to thrive.


In community,
Shabd Simon-Alexander

[Official attachment page break]

I am writing today in support of Commercial Rent Stabilization. Nine years ago, I started a
fashion line in NYC. I had very little money and support around me and very little knowledge
about starting a business. I ran my business out of my apartment in Brooklyn, often competing
for space with my young child. If I had the opportunity to afford space outside of my home, it
would have been a game changer for my business. I often had to have models visit my home for
fittings, which wasn’t professional. When MTV did a piece on me, they came to my apartment
and rearranged my furniture to make it look like I had a full studio. I was also spending lots of
money hiring transportation to take me from the garment district to my apartment with loads of
fabric, materials, etc because it was too far for me to carry on my own. If I had been able to
afford space in the garment district, my business would have gone much further and it would
have afforded me the space to dedicate to creating.

Thank you,

Tabitha St. Bernard-Jacobs
Founder,
Tabii Just Clothing

TESTIMONY IN SUPPORT OF COMMERCIAL RENT STABILIZATION
WITH RECOMMENDATIONS TO UPDATE THE LEGISLATION
9/17/21
Vanessa Thill, [public-safety redaction: email] ([public-safety redaction: street address] 11205)


When a working-class neighborhood is targeted for speculative development, commercial
tenants have little protection against the inevitable onslaught of rent increases and harassment
by landlords and developers who are looking to cash in. This lack of protection allows for the
rapid dismantling of working-class neighborhoods’ social infrastructure. An entire safety net and
cultural community can be liquidated at the drop of a hat. Small businesses are more than just
storefronts. They are often part of networks of community organizations, social services,
cooperative spaces, and cultural venues. Small businesses can also provide an alternative
means of subsistence for people who face limited opportunities and discrimination in the labor
market due to immigration status, or other factors.


Over the last 13 years, I have experienced the disastrous impacts of the lack of protections first
hand. As an artist, I rent commercial studio space as part of my livelihood. Rampant speculation
has made it such that I have only been able to afford basement studio spaces over the last 9
years. As we saw with Hurricane Ida, the total unregulation of real estate is so extreme that it
literally displaces people underground, forcing people such as myself to sacrifice health and
well-being in order to afford rent.


We had Commercial Rent Control in NYC from 1945-1963 until the real estate lobby killed it.
I urge you to support Intro 1796, but I urge you to go further than what has been proposed,
knowing that landlords and developers will take advantage of any loophole you leave open.
Below are my recommendations.


Recommendations:
   -   Rent Guidelines Board appointee requirements:
           -   The chair must have 5 years of expertise in community development or
               community organizing, in addition to finance and economics.
           -   The members representing commercial tenants should not represent chain
               businesses.

[Official attachment page break]

-   The public members should not be commercial landlords.
       -   Mayoral appointment and removal of board members should be subject to city
           council approval.
-   Combat inflation before rates are locked-in
       -   The initial rent for an occupied space should be the rent on the day the law is
           passed, not the day it becomes effective (otherwise landlords will raise rents in
           the interim).
       -   Since the initial rent for a vacant space is essentially at the discretion of the
           landlord, there should be a robust appeal process in place.
       -   Tenants and owners should have 60 days after the notice of initial registration to
           file for an adjustment of the rent, with an opportunity for the other party to
           respond.
-   City government must specify and oversee administration and enforcement agency
       -   Require landlords to register lease and all riders to the enforcement agency
           (failure to do so results in penalties). Treat missing registration as amended
           registration resulting in a rent freeze.
       -   The rent on the lease, the rent actually paid, and the rent in the registration
           should match or the registration should not be accepted for filing.
       -   The enforcement agency should send a complete rent history to the tenant every
           year. The rent history should include, if applicable, any overcharges, rent
           adjustments won through appeals or court cases, the effective date of any new
           and collectible rents, and any tax benefits or financing programs that apply to the
           building.
       -   Establish a standard vacancy lease format to be used by all landlords when
           applicable
       -   In case of an overcharge, the registration statements that include overcharges
           should be invalidated and the landlord must correct all fraudulent registrations.
           The lookback period for bringing overcharge complaints should be as long as
           possible, and overcharges should be met with fines and civil penalties.
       -   Rents should be frozen after any year where a registration is missing, false, or
           incomplete. The freeze should be lifted only when all missing registrations are
           filed and all false registrations are corrected.
-   Add Right to Renew & long lease options to the bill

Testimony of Laura Wolf-Powers on
Int 1796-2019, Regulation of Commercial Rent
September 17, 2021
New York City Council Committee on Small Business (Virtual Hearing)


I am here today to testify in support of Int 1796-2019, a bill that would address
the crisis of attrition facing small, locally owned retail, commercial and industrial
businesses in New York City by establishing a long-overdue system of commercial
rent registration and regulation. I am an Associate Professor of Urban Policy and
Planning at Hunter College, part of the City University of New York. I have been
teaching and studying community & economic development at the graduate level
for two decades, and I acted as an informal consultant on Comptroller Scott
Stringer’s 2019 study of retail vacancy in the city. The views I am expressing here
are my own and not those of my employer.
Recently, I had the chance to re-watch the 2012 documentary My Brooklyn, which
chronicles the city-sponsored transformation of downtown Brooklyn’s
commercial and retail landscape during the administration of Michael Bloomberg.
I have seen this film many times before and I regularly show it to students; every
single time, it delivers a gut punch, making me sad and angry in equal parts. The
film tells the story of a community of entrepreneurs in the Fulton Mall area who
bore the consequences of decisions by policymakers and legislators to put the
interests of property owners over the stability of a thriving retail district, to put
the interests of property owners over the economic well-being of small business
proprietors who were predominantly immigrants and people of color, to put the
interests of property owners over the interests of the low and middle income
consumers who came from all over the borough because they loved and
appreciated the culture of the place and its concentration of products they
wanted to buy at prices they could afford. Downtown Brooklyn is now dominated
by generic chain retail - and riddled with vacancies. Dozens of locally owned
businesses have been displaced by high rent. Many of the small businesses that
remain are struggling and uncertain about the future. This scenario is repeated on
community retail corridors all across the city. Looking back on the City Council’s

[Official attachment page break]

decision to approve a fateful rezoning for downtown Brooklyn in 2005, now-
former City Councilman Charles Barron told the filmmaker bluntly, “we should
have said no.”

The bill under consideration here is a chance to say “yes” to a new system of
regulation that can stabilize the city’s small businesses and small business districts
at this crucial moment, the same way residential rent regulation stabilizes
households and neighborhoods. The small businesses that have survived the
COVID crisis of the last 18 months desperately need relief from untenable rent
costs – rents that far exceed what is necessary to maintain their properties and
deliver a reasonable return on investment to the property owner. Furthermore,
community members should not have to worry that landlords will evict the local
businesses they love and depend upon and leave their space vacant for months
and years as they warehouse real estate in anticipation of chain store tenants.

A fair and just recovery from COVID in New York City depends on stability for our
neighborhood businesses. Please pass Intro 1796 now.

Charlotta Janssen, owner of Chez Oskar in Bed Stuy and member of the Bed Stuy
Restaurant Association.Restaurant tenants' number one problem are landlords. Every
Realtor boasts about us neighborhood restaurants when they sell real estate. Look up any
site and you will find mine. Those same realtors are fighting this desperately needed bill and
I would like for none of these realtors here to speak on our behalf.

1998 I opened Chez Oskar in Fort Greene. Crime was high and we were glad if we even had
10 customers. We had put everything into this business. With our neighbors we became
Fort Greene's restaurant row and felt a great sense of community, helping each other with
napkins, tablecloths, soda gas and more. Slowly all those pioneers that made Fort Greene
vibrant and multicultural have disappeared. None of the original businesses are still there -
each (including me) had a painful eviction.

My team is my family. Oskar's chef, Octavio Simanacas, is with me since 1999, my GM
Angelique Calmet Strakker since 2002. In 2012 I realized my landlord was ripping me off on
taxes and water bills. When confronted he said: "that's it, I'll never give you another lease" &
when my lease was up he evicted.


In Fort Greene I had nothing to show for 18 years of really good business, no equity at all.
My landlord sold my kitchen for scrap, collected key money and had a tenant paying more
than double what I did.


Most landlords do this, they destroy community for money, make running small bizzes,
family restaurants & dining out unaffordable.

We restaurants invest hundreds of thousands of dollars to open and when our leases are up
we can’t take it with us, nor do we have any way to continue in the communities we helped
build. Every realtor loves to boast of the diverse restaurants that make communities vibrant
& those are the first to evict us.

In Bed Stuy I am the only surviving business on my block because I now own. Many dreams
are shattered, now giant debts, while landlords have mortgages on pause and wait for the
next sucker to charge key money & double rent, oh and add on roadside, for which we, not
they, fought.

Businesses, that invest into a place as much as restaurants do, from sweat equity to solid
infrastructure, need rent stabilization like in France. There a commercial lease is a lease for
life, much like once a taxi medallion.

[Official attachment page break]

Let's clarify gentrification: there are communifiers and commodifiers:
Communifiers invest themselves and do their best to give services that improve life in their
communities.
Commodifiers calculate how little they have to give and how much they can pull out of their
community: keep empty storefronts, overcharge and bring in chain stores. The less they
give the more they will be rewarded.

We need laws that differentiate between the two. small businesses that work hard, invest
themselves into communities should not be thrown out to benefit commodifiers/landlords,
shattering small business dream.

Commercial Rent Stabilization works. That is why Paris isn’t a ghost town, but NYC is. Let‘s
make Paris in New York!

That means it's not a rent freeze. Ask me—it's not permanent. It is a board that's making a decision, rather than individuals or LLCs, let's be real. And it's going to enforce compliance through strong penalty provisions against overcharges and tenant harassment. Tenant harassment is one of the biggest issues my office has heard about from commercial landlords, and that is something we absolutely must put a stop to.

So it does not freeze rents entirely or roll back existing rents. It does not prevent landlords from making a fair return. And it does not apply retroactively to existing leases.

So I have a lot that I owe to the next speaker, because while Assembly Member Gallagher and Senator Salazar—we've picked this bill up this last year to fight for its passage, and we will win—this bill has been fought for for a while, and Olympia Kazi has been at the forefront of that fight. And you will see why when you hear her speak.

Hi.

Small Business United will never be defeated!
Small Business United will never be defeated!
Small Business United will never be defeated!

And that reminds me that Alison and her organization, Small Business United—you can sign up. They have a great website. They are fighting for this bill, and they are welcoming every small business that wants to be involved, as well as people who love small businesses, which would include all of us. So please check them out and get signed up so that you can continue to be in the fight with us.

Now, as we know, this is a big systemic issue that we are taking on. We are taking on Goliath with this Goliath, but every single little fight matters, and every single little fight is a huge fight in this, because every single little fight is a community that we are defending.

And I am so proud to stand with Jimmy's Corner, one of my favorite bars, and I'm going to hand it over to Adam to wrap us up.

speakers.name: Alison Hirsh
speakers.scope_note: Complete attributed rally statement.

turns.text:
Hey, everybody. My name is Alison Hirsh, and I'm here with Action Lab and Small Business United.

Small Business United is a new organization made up of small business owners, for small business owners, in New York City. We talk a lot about the affordability crisis in New York City, but all too often we forget that small businesses are a huge component of what it means for people in New York City to be able to have economic mobility, to build a life here, and to build a community and neighborhood.

And all too often, because of people like Durst and companies like Durst, small businesses are thrown aside, and the communities that rely on them are worse off because of it.

So Small Business United is super proud to be here standing with Adam and Jimmy's Corner, with Assembly Member Gallagher and Senator Salazar, who are sponsoring Small Business rent stabilization in Albany and are 100% committed to seeing this fight through—both for businesses like Jimmy's Corner, for folks like Freddy, who you'll hear from later, who runs a restaurant in Jackson Heights, and for businesses all over New York City who need people to stand up and say small businesses are a core part of what make our neighborhoods special and unique, and we're going to continue fighting for them.

So thank you all for being here, and thank you so much.

speakers.name: Julia Salazar
speakers.role_at_event: New York State Senator and S8319 prime sponsor
speakers.current_context: Same office and sponsorship role as of 2026-07-28.
speakers.scope_note: Complete attributed rally statement.

turns.text:
Thank you so much, Assembly Member Gallagher. Good morning, everyone.

What a beautiful crowd we have out here for Jimmy's and for commercial rent stabilization. I am Senator Julia Salazar. I represent New York's 18th District in Brooklyn and Queens, but I am here today to support Jimmy's Corner, both as a patron but also as the Senate sponsor of the Small Business Rent Stabilization Act.

The great late Jimmy Glenn opened Jimmy's Corner back in 1971, way before Times Square was the neighborhood that it is today. Jimmy created a space where everyone would be welcome and where locals could actually afford to spend time. Today, Jimmy's is one of the last true dive bars left in this area.

The size of the crowd here demonstrates that there is a community surrounding this beloved business, which you heard Adam speak to. There is a community who doesn't want to see this special place be forced out. The impact that Jimmy's Corner and the Glenn family have had here is one that corporate chains could never replicate.

Many of the surrounding businesses have already either been forced to close or they've had to raise their prices astronomically to keep up with their costs. While we are here rallying to save Jimmy's, this problem is bigger than a single bar. This is about the fact that small businesses are being squeezed out of our city. Across every borough, community-oriented businesses are shutting down because their rents are rising to levels that only national chains can afford.

Commercial landlords are keeping storefronts empty as they wait for a higher-paying tenant to come along, rather than renting the space sooner to a local business owner. Our streets are losing the character that small businesses give us, replaced by corporate malls lined with Sweetgreen and Starbucks.

Just the other day, I passed a space in Brooklyn where Gino's Pizza used to be. A real estate company bought their building and raised the monthly rent from $10,000 a month to $25,000 a month. It's a shame. That's a 150% increase.

This is a culture crisis, an economic crisis. Nearly half of our state's workforce is employed by small businesses. When those businesses are forced to shut down, New Yorkers lose their jobs.

We need small business rent stabilization to save our local businesses. This bill would limit unaffordable rent hikes. It would guarantee lease renewals, and it would protect at-will tenants.

We will continue to fight for commercial rent stabilization. We will continue to fight for Jimmy's Corner and for every business that is struggling in our city and our state. Thank you.

speakers.name: Emelyn Stuart
speakers.scope_note: Complete attributed rally statement.

turns.text:
Hello, everyone. I am Emelyn Stuart, the first Afro-Latina to own a movie theater here in New York.

And so I built the theater in 2018, and in 2023 I decided I wanted to expand and build a theater in Sunset Park, my childhood neighborhood. And so I signed a 10-year lease, and I started working and hired architects and electricians and spent a ton of money, and three months later I was locked out of the space because the landlord had lost the building in an auction because he owed back taxes.

And things like this happen all the time. Most recently, at my existing theater, I expanded and added an auditorium. I spent almost $200,000 building this auditorium, and two months after I opened it, I got a 60-day eviction notice because the building had been sold.

And this is happening to many, many businesses in New York.

And we're not saying that commercial landlords shouldn't raise the rent. We get it. We have expenses too. We get that. What we're saying is we need better, fair practices. We need people to understand that small businesses—every time I am affected as a small business, my employees are affected. My community is affected.

This bill is super important. We need guardrails for the commercial landlords. Thank you.

speakers.name: Tony Simone
speakers.role_at_event: New York State Assembly Member and A5568A co-sponsor
speakers.current_context: Same office and co-sponsor role as of 2026-07-28.
speakers.scope_note: Complete attributed rally statement.

turns.text:
Hi, everyone. Thank you all for being here. I want to thank the sponsors of this amazing bill, Assembly Member Emily Gallagher and my friend Julia Salazar from the State Senate. I'm also joined by my amazing colleague, Assembly Member Jo Anne Simon. They also often mix up our names.

But look, small business is the heart and soul of New York City, whether it's our bodegas, whether it's our dive bars. Who doesn't love a dive bar where you can still afford to drink a beer in Jimmy's?

If you want soulless corporate lobbies, move to Houston. No offense, but this is New York City. We don't need 10 Sweetgreens. We don't need 100 corporate-owned businesses. We need these small businesses to make New York City for who we are.

And it is a crime that you can raise the rent 100%, 200%, and then you have these empty storefronts. One of the biggest issues that came before me when I was a candidate, by folks in Hell's Kitchen and Chelsea, was: why are these storefronts so empty for so long? Why?

And we talked to the landlords, and we talked to the banks, like, "Oh, well, the market says, the market says." But clearly the market is broken. It's corporate greed, and it's capitalism run amok. So it's not working for our communities.

And look, with the onset of AI, we're going to be in a big fight for jobs. These small bodegas, these dive bars—they employ people from the community and real New Yorkers, and that's why I'm a big supporter of the Commercial Rent Stabilization Act.

We have to ensure that landlords cannot raise the rent so quickly simply because of greed, simply because they can. They need to have a heart again, and if not, we're going to go after them.

So I stand here proudly. Thank you for inviting me. Welcome to my district. Go have a beer at Jimmy's. We need to save Jimmy's bar—save Jimmy's—and we have to ensure that we pass this Commercial Rent Stabilization Act.

speakers.name: Freddy Castiblanco
speakers.scope_note: Complete attributed rally statement.

turns.text:
Yes, good morning, distinguished members of the New York State Legislature. My name is Freddy Castiblanco. I'm a physician and Colombian immigrant. I came to this country 26 years ago with the firm conviction that honest work and commitment to community could build something lasting for everyone.

Twenty-five years ago, I founded Terraza 7 in Queens. My business, my dream, has developed into what is today an artistic and cultural landmark of New York City. In this space, we have presented more than 7,000 concerts that tell the story of the Americas through music and show how migration, and in particular the African diaspora, have built the musical soul of an entire continent—from Morocco and Andalucía, through the Caribbean and the sounds of Veracruz, all the way to jazz, cumbia, samba, candombe, and tango.

But Terraza 7 has not only been a stage for that musical phenomenon. It also has been a platform for justice. We have fought for workers' rights, for [unclear] leave, for thousands of New Yorkers who need it, and testified before Congress in support of the Affordable Care Act with a public option.

We have always believed that community business has an obligation to fight for the dignity of everyone involved in it and around it.

But despite all that work, that commitment, and love for this city, I have come close to losing Terraza three times—not for lack of effort, not for lack of community support, but because landlords who witnessed our success decided that our success was their opportunity, that what we built over years through sweat, sacrifice, and community trust could be turned into profit for them.

Overnight, my rent went up from $7,500 to $12,500 a month, nearly double the industry standard, even in the middle of the pandemic when our doors were shut and our community was suffering. I had no way to pay such an exorbitant amount, so I was taken to court and faced $150,000 in back charges. I have spent years and thousands of dollars raised from this very community simply to keep the doors of Terraza open.

That is not a market failure. That is an injustice. And I am not the only one with such a story. All across New York City, the independent businesses that give our neighborhoods their soul are disappearing, replaced by chains that can afford the high rent but contribute nothing to the distinctive culture and human fabric of the community that we are losing forever.

When a bodega closes its doors, when a family restaurant shuts down, when a music venue goes dark, it's not just a business that disappears. A piece of neighborhood identity dies with it, and that will never come back.

This is why I stand with Small Business United today and urge you to pass the Small Business Rent Stabilization Act, which will establish a commercial rent regulation board to set fair limits on annual rent increases and will guarantee the right to lease renewal so that small businesses can plan, invest, and grow without fear of being displaced overnight by the unilateral decision of a single powerful landlord.

Nearly 90% of new jobs annually in this city are created by small businesses, and New York's neighborhoods are defined by their people and by their local businesses. Without commercial rent protection, we will lose both.

I'm asking you to pass this law not only for Terraza 7, but for every business that is experiencing today what I have gone through, and for those that do not yet know what awaits them if we don't act now.

Please pass the Small Business Rent Stabilization Act. The future of spaces like ours, and of the communities that sustain them—and that they, in turn, sustain—depends on what we and you decide today. Thank you.

speakers.name: Jo Anne Simon
speakers.role_at_event: New York State Assembly Member and A5568A co-sponsor
speakers.current_context: Same office and co-sponsor role as of 2026-07-28.
speakers.scope_note: Complete attributed rally statement.

turns.text:
Thank you, Emily. And thank you, Senator Salazar as well, and the other speakers.

You know, Emily mentioned something that has been happening in my district for a long time, and that is when somebody comes in and they decide to capitalize on the work that community has done—setting down those roots, keeping those thriving businesses going. And you know, as I have said at plenty of opportunities, you are here because we were there at the time, right?

And so a couple of things that are not just about small business, but about the history of New York: our small businesses were really critical pieces of the history of New York. One of the dive bars in my community that opened in [public-safety redaction: street address] where the steel workers, who were Mohawks from upstate, came, and they built the Empire State Building, right? They were the high-steel workers, and this was their place, and that is a critical, important historical fact in our city's history.

And also Montero's, which is now only 90 years old, just got bought over by somebody who promises to keep it what it was. It was the longshoremen's bar and still looks like it was the longshoremen's bar. They haven't done anything to it, and it's great, and everybody loves it and still populates it.

But it's also those delis. The delis that used to be the safe haven, the refuge—if you were being followed by somebody, you could go into that deli. And those were delis that often fed some of the homeless people in our communities as well, on a regular basis, and they were very integral parts.

And so one down the corner from me is now a very fancy, shishi place. They got more than twice the rent. And nobody goes into that place. Lovely windows, very nicely laid out, but nobody goes into that place, and it's soulless, and it's a vacant, dead corner of the block that used to be very alive.

So it's about our communities. It's about our small businesses. It's about the role they play in our community, the business life of our city, and the history of our city, that we need to protect these businesses and keep them from being displaced.

So thank you very much for your support, and thank you to Emily.

speakers.name: Jamell Henderson
speakers.scope_note: Complete attributed rally statement.

turns.text:
Good morning, New York City.

First of all, it's truly an honor to be here, and I want to say thank you to the Black business owners across Brooklyn who trusted me to be a stand for them in this time, because they are right now fighting hard to keep their businesses open.

Let me give you a few: [unclear business name], Kombi Lounge, Savannah Spice, Cold Peppers, Sugarcane BK—these are just some of the Black businesses that have been closed, not because of economic development within the community, but because the prices are so outrageously high they had no other choice but to either relocate or close their business permanently, losing their mark in the neighborhood for decades. Is that fair? And that's right.

You have businesses right now like Nicholas BK in Bed-Stuy, [Lacou/Lacoux] Cafe in Crown Heights, that are fighting hard to hold on because the landlords are charging them outrageous prices, and it is not fair to them, nor to the people that are supporting them.

And I'm here to say, on behalf of the Black businesses across Brooklyn and the state of New York, we're tired of it, and we are so proud to stand with my friends, authentic leaders who are taking this challenge to be so important. Because let's be real: who's trying to pay $15 for a Heineken, right? Who's trying to pay $25 for a Hennessy and ginger ale when you have local neighborhood businesses like Jimmy's Corner, where I've told plenty of stories from when I was a grad student at Baruch College? Because when I was working on my capstone, I needed a drink, and I went to Jimmy's Corner—part of the many stories where I'm a four-time CUNY grad today.

But the point is that I'm here to stand with our Assembly members, because we're going to bring this across the finish line. Because guess what? There are groups like Kwanzaa Crawl. We're getting ready to have a spring edition of Kwanzaa Crawl this June 6. Groups like this are making sure that they drive economic development to businesses that are struggling, but they shouldn't have to do that when we have the power to change government right now.

So I'm asking all of you to stand with me. Members of the press, connect with Black businesses that are waiting to hear from you, that are waiting to tell their story, so we can bring this home across the finish line and keep progressives in New York State.

Thank you so much.

speakers.name: Lindsey Boylan
speakers.role_at_event: Candidate for New York City Council District 3
speakers.current_context: Role recorded as of the event.
speakers.scope_note: Complete attributed rally statement.

turns.text:
You got to give it up to our two co-sponsors of this bill. They are incredible women, and they're not just doing this for the whole state—they're doing this for the city.

When this legislation passes, we will create so much opportunity. Look right behind us: "Retail available." I did not order that sign today, but that is exactly what you get in this environment. Without this bill, you get not only "retail available"—look around you, every single thing you see is a bank. We do not need another retail bank.

And if you don't have one of these two things—I live in Chelsea, our great leader Tony Simone was just talking about our Hell's Kitchen and Chelsea neighborhoods—so many empty storefronts. The corner of my block has been empty for years. Just down the block from that, an entire swath, especially new building, new construction.

Especially now that we have an incoming wave of new build in this city, we need to protect the future of small business.

I'll also say, having done economic development at the state, the idea that this somehow harms our economy is the exact perversion of reality. Small business is what creates new jobs, is what creates the economic opportunity, is what creates the future for our city. It's not the big businesses. It's not the national anchor tenants that we have that are giving more opportunity and giving it to more people. It is our small businesses. It's the Jimmy's Corner.

And so I couldn't be more proud to be here today. The only thing I'll say is: at night, these banks are all closed. "Retail available"—that's not opening up. It's our neighborhood tenants. It's our neighborhood businesses that keep us safe, that keep neighborhoods positive and progressing, employ our people, and it's the only way forward for a safe and quality-of-life New York City.

So I'm so excited to support. Thank you so much.

speakers.name: Olympia Kazi
speakers.role_at_event: NYC Artist Coalition co-founder and Commercial Rent Stabilization advocate
speakers.scope_note: Complete attributed rally statement.

turns.text:
Everybody, you know why we're all here on this sunny day: because we're fed up. That's right. This is not fair.

We sit on the backs of giants. This business was started by Adam's dad 54 years ago. Guess what else was happening 54 years ago? A young person named Ruth Messinger—some of you may have heard of her—was working on a commercial rent stabilization bill, and it hasn't happened. And why hasn't it happened? Because our leaders haven't had the pressure that you are hearing today.

Okay, our voices need to be heard. The fact that we don't have a microphone is not a problem, as you can see. The only problem that we have is people of privilege who don't want to be taxed around this time at the budget, and they don't want the tilted scales to be fixed.

We are not asking anything radical. We're not asking anything radical. What we are asking is a basic protection. What this bill does is a basic protection.

We build the success. We build the community. We make the culture that generates millions for the Real Estate Board, and we are happy for them to take their millions, but we ask for our fair share, right? We said it right: our success is not yours to go all the way to the bank laughing on our account because we're disempowered.

We have leadership at the state. And I want to talk about what is happening now. The real culprit here is Governor Hochul. It's going to be Mayor Mamdani. It's going to be Speaker Menin. Speaker Menin was the chair of the Small Business Committee when she was a council member, and this bill went in front of her. Did we even get a hearing from her? We didn't. And now she can allow it to be introduced at the city.

But guess what? We're going to pass it in the state. We're going to pass it in the city. Because what is happening right now is very, very sad. Actually, it's worse than what Emily said. Emily said, "Oh, they're waiting for a corporate tenant that is going to give you more money." Here is the sad truth: real estate has been financialized to that level that they don't even want a tenant. They just say, "This lease is $50,000 now. I'm never going to find any idiot to give me $50,000, but what I can do is state that in my bank and get a loan of the equivalent of whatever number makes sense on the paper."

But it doesn't make sense for us. It doesn't make sense for the families. I'm also a mother of two kids, and we need to change this. It cannot be another generation that suffers through that, right?

So it doesn't make sense for the people that, as Julia said, employ more than 50% of our workforce. It doesn't make sense for the people that give us affordable services. When we talk about affordability, it is not just a slogan for people to win elections. Affordability is about displacement, and not just housing displacement. There is secondary displacement, because if your house is protected, but you can't afford to do anything in your neighborhood anymore—if you don't feel welcome going into businesses like in the stories that you heard—how is this not an issue of affordability and displacement?

And then, last but not least, all my life I work for culture. I feel culture is what unites us. Community comes through culture, and our small businesses are the best ambassadors of our culture, and it's high time that we're going to save them.

And I want to thank also Small Business United that is taking the mantle and organizing people, because with Action Lab support and with its amazing leaders at this stage, we are going to pass commercial rent stabilization.

records.name: Julia Salazar
records.role_at_statement: New York State Senator and S8319 prime sponsor
records.text: The Small Business Survival Act would be a lifeline for small businesses in New York City by capping outrageous rent hikes and guaranteeing lease renewals. Corporate landlords are charging rents so high that the only business owners who can afford to pay are corporate chains. Or, they’re keeping storefronts vacant until larger, wealthier tenants come along. This is a toxic and now commonplace pattern that is shuttering our local businesses, putting New Yorkers out of work, and turning our vibrant neighborhoods into chain malls.

records.name: Emily Gallagher
records.role_at_statement: New York State Assembly Member and A5568A prime sponsor
records.text: Small businesses are what make New York special, but they are increasingly being pushed out by greedy corporate actors. In the 20 years I’ve been in my neighborhood, I’ve seen so many beloved businesses close because of unaffordable rents or because big landlords would rather wait for a corporate chain to come along. With the Small Business Survival Act, we will cap rent, guarantee leases, and ensure our community businesses are actually owned by the members of our community.

records.name: Olympia Kazi
records.text: I want to thank State Senator Julia Salazar and Assembly Member Emily Gallagher for introducing this critical legislation to enact a common-sense, fundamental protection for commercial tenants. For more than half a century, communities have fought to defend beloved small businesses, nonprofits, and cultural institutions from displacement and erasure. With renewed leadership in New York State and New York City that centers affordability and justice, I am hopeful—and confident—that the moment to pass commercial rent stabilization has arrived.

records.name: Small Business United
records.text: Small businesses are struggling to survive in New York City because they cannot keep up with continuously rising costs, including the rising cost of rent. This crisis is the result of treating commercial space as a commodity to make corporate real estate companies richer, rather than as community infrastructure to support our neighborhoods. New York must pass the Small Business Survival Act before our local business owners are forced to close their doors and seek opportunities elsewhere.
